questions.q: What is the Automated Test Framework (ATF)?
options: A native, built-in ServiceNow capability for automated UI and server-side regression testing — not an external tool
A third-party plugin that must be purchased from the marketplace before it can be used
A manual checklist admins fill out after every deployment
A reporting dashboard that only displays past Change Request outcomes
questions.explain: ATF ships with the platform itself, built on the platform the same way any other application is.

questions.q: Why does Course 6's low-code customization (Business Rules, Client Scripts, UI Policies, Flows) create a real risk of silent regressions?
options: A small configuration change can affect behavior far outside the form where it was written, with no syntax error to flag it
Low-code customizations are always rejected automatically before they can run
Business Rules and Client Scripts cannot run on any table other than the one they were written for
Low-code changes are inherently safer than any other kind of platform change
questions.explain: A Business Rule or UI Policy can quietly interact with other features on the same table, and nothing about that interaction throws an error.

questions.q: What are the two core building blocks ATF is made of?
options: Test Steps (individual reusable actions) and Tests (an ordered sequence of Test Steps)
Change Requests and Update Sets
Business Rules and Client Scripts
Dev instances and Prod instances
questions.explain: A single Test Step does little on its own; a Test strings several together into one real scenario.

questions.q: When does ATF's value actually show up, according to this lesson?
options: In the gap between making a change and promoting it to production, before the change goes live
Only after a change has already caused a production incident
Only during the initial platform implementation, never afterward
ATF provides no particular benefit tied to timing
questions.explain: Running a Test Suite against a Test environment before a Change Request is approved catches regressions while they're still cheap to fix.

questions.q: How does a Test differ from a Test Step?
options: A Test is a sequence of Test Steps run in order that together simulate one full scenario; a Test Step is one small individual action
A Test Step always contains multiple full Tests inside it
There is no real difference — the two terms describe the same record type
A Test can only be built from server-side logic, never from UI actions
questions.explain: Test Steps are the reusable building blocks; a Test is what strings them together into a real end-to-end scenario.
